Two years ago our island's committee asked the ferry operator one question: why does the middle of the timetable move every day? The answer turned out to be the most useful thing anybody has told us about our own harbour. Every crossing waits for a window of deep water, the windows drift by fifty minutes a day, and so the only honest timetable is one that drifts with them. Oskar Lind 3d
Every morning for a month I counted the people who walked down to the slipway for the midday boat and turned round at the top of the hill when they saw the queue. It was never fewer than six and once it was nineteen, most of them with shopping and two with a pram, and not one of them would ever have shown up in the operator's numbers, because nobody counts the passengers who give up before they get to the boat. That is the number I am taking to the meeting on Thursday.

The keeper's last entry for that winter is eleven words long, and it gives the wind, the barometer and the hour the glass went before anything else, as every entry before it had. His daughter found the book forty years later in a trunk in the byre, under a coil of rope and a box of lamp glasses, and read it through in one night by the light of the kitchen stove, and she said afterwards that she had never known him at all until then...

What the keeper wrote

A lighthouse keeper's logs are mostly about the weather and the household, not the light. Volunteers from the history society have spent two winters transcribing the four hundred pages he wrote in the year the causeway flooded, and the library is showing a selection of them from Monday, together with the tide tables and the ration books of that year and a map of the island as it was before the causeway was built across the sound.
